quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: In a job interview, the very first question is 'so, tell me about yourself.' What should the answer avoid leading with?
quests.correctAnswer: A full chronological work history - that answer is a common trap that rarely gets to what actually matters for this specific role.
quests.hint: This question is often a trap for a rambling autobiography - resist that pull.
quests.explanation: The most common answer to this question is also the weakest one - a chronological history says little about fit for this specific role.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Answer 'tell me about yourself' for a candidate applying to a data analyst role, in a way that's focused and relevant rather than chronological.
quests.correctAnswer: I spend most of my time finding the one number in a messy dataset that actually explains why something happened - that's what pulled me into analytics in the first place.
quests.hint: Lead with what you actually do and care about, not a timeline of jobs held.
quests.explanation: Leading with a focused thread of what you do and value, rather than a timeline, gives the interviewer something specific to follow up on.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The interviewer follows up with 'and what got you into that?' Give a brief, genuine answer that deepens the pitch without derailing into a full life story.
quests.correctAnswer: Honestly, a messy spreadsheet at my first job that nobody else wanted to untangle - I found I actually enjoyed it.
quests.hint: Keep the follow-up short, specific, and genuine.
quests.explanation: A brief, specific follow-up keeps the momentum of the pitch going, rather than letting it sprawl once given an opening.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: At a professional networking event, what's a common mistake people make in their opening self-introduction?
quests.correctAnswer: Leading entirely with a job title and company name, which rarely gives the other person anything to actually respond to.
quests.hint: A title alone tends to end a conversation rather than open one.
quests.explanation: The goal of a networking introduction is to start a conversation, not to file a complete report on your employment status.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Introduce yourself at a networking event as a product manager at a mid-size logistics company, in a way that invites conversation rather than closing it.
quests.correctAnswer: I spend my days figuring out why a delivery that should take two days sometimes takes five, and fixing that.
quests.hint: Describe what you actually do in practice, in a way that invites a follow-up question.
quests.explanation: Describing the actual work, rather than the title, gives the listener something concrete to react to or ask about.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The person you're talking to says 'oh, that sounds frustrating to untangle - how do you even start?' Answer briefly, keeping the conversation open rather than over-explaining.
quests.correctAnswer: Usually it's one broken handoff between two systems that don't talk to each other well - find that, and most of the rest sorts itself out.
quests.hint: Give a genuinely interesting but brief answer, leaving room for the conversation to keep going.
quests.explanation: A brief, genuinely interesting answer keeps a networking conversation alive far longer than a complete, exhaustive explanation would.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You're pitching an internal proposal to your department head for extending team working hours flexibility. What should the pitch lead with: your personal preference, or the department's actual interest?
quests.correctAnswer: The department's actual interest - a proposal framed around personal preference is a much harder case to make than one framed around shared benefit.
quests.hint: An internal proposal usually needs to serve the department's interest to get approved, not just the proposer's.
quests.explanation: Framing a personal-benefit request in terms of departmental value is often what actually gets it approved, regardless of the real motivation behind it.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch that flexible-hours proposal to your department head, framed around the department's benefit.
quests.correctAnswer: A few people on the team do their best focused work early morning, others late - letting hours flex a bit would likely mean more actual output, not less.
quests.hint: Frame the proposal entirely around departmental output, not personal convenience.
quests.explanation: This is the same skill as pitching a product to a manager earlier in the curriculum, applied to a proposal about your own working conditions.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Your department head asks 'how would we make sure people are still available for meetings?' Answer that practical concern directly, keeping the proposal moving forward.
quests.correctAnswer: Core meeting hours would stay fixed, say ten to two - flexibility would only apply outside that window, so availability wouldn't actually change.
quests.hint: Address the specific practical concern with a concrete, workable answer.
quests.explanation: Anticipating and directly answering the practical objection a decision-maker will actually have is what turns a good idea into an approved one.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You're introducing a new project to your team for the first time. What should the opening focus on: the project's full scope, or why it matters to them?
quests.correctAnswer: Why it matters to them - a full scope dump upfront tends to overwhelm before the team has any reason to care about the details.
quests.hint: Earning the team's interest usually comes before dumping every detail of scope.
quests.explanation: Motivation before mechanics is a pattern that holds true whether you're pitching a product to a stranger or a project to your own team.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Introduce a new internal project - rebuilding the customer onboarding flow - to your team, leading with why it matters rather than the full technical scope.
quests.correctAnswer: Right now, a third of new customers drop off before they even finish setting up - this project is about fixing that specific leak.
quests.hint: Lead with the real, motivating reason the project exists.
quests.explanation: Starting with the actual problem the project solves gives the team a reason to care before they're asked to absorb any scope details.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A team member asks 'how much of my time is this going to take?' Answer that practical concern honestly and specifically.
quests.correctAnswer: Realistically, a few focused hours a week for the first month, then it tapers off once the core flow's rebuilt.
quests.hint: Give an honest, specific time estimate rather than a vague reassurance.
quests.explanation: A specific, honest time estimate respects a team member's real planning needs far more than a vague 'not too much' would.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: In a first meeting with a new potential client, should the pitch open with your company's history, or with the client's specific situation?
quests.correctAnswer: The client's specific situation - opening with your own history before understanding theirs tends to feel self-centered rather than helpful.
quests.hint: A first client meeting usually goes better when it starts by understanding them, not by presenting yourself.
quests.explanation: Leading with genuine curiosity about the client's situation, rather than your own history, sets a collaborative tone from the very first minute.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Open a first meeting with a potential marketing client by asking about their specific situation rather than presenting your agency first.
quests.correctAnswer: Before I walk you through anything, tell me - what's actually not working right now with your current marketing that made you take this meeting?
quests.hint: Open with a genuine question about their situation, not a company pitch.
quests.explanation: Opening with a real question, rather than a rehearsed pitch, often produces more useful information and a stronger eventual pitch.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The client answers that their ads get clicks but rarely convert into sales. Pitch your agency's specific relevant strength in response to exactly that answer.
quests.correctAnswer: That's actually our specialty - most agencies chase clicks, we focus on what happens after the click, which is usually where the real money's being lost.
quests.hint: Build the pitch directly from what the client just revealed, rather than a generic capabilities overview.
quests.explanation: A pitch built from what the client just said, rather than a rehearsed capabilities list, feels immediately relevant instead of generic.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A freelance writer is cold-emailing a potential client. What's the risk of opening with a long list of past clients and credentials?
quests.correctAnswer: The client may not read past the first line if it's not clearly relevant to their specific need.
quests.hint: A cold outreach message has to earn attention in its first line, not its tenth.
quests.explanation: In cold outreach, the first line has to do more work than in any other context, because there's no existing relationship keeping the listener engaged.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Write the opening line of a cold outreach message from a freelance writer to a small business whose blog hasn't been updated in six months.
quests.correctAnswer: Noticed your blog's been quiet since spring - happy to help if you're looking to get it moving again.
quests.hint: Open with something specific and true about their situation, not your own credentials.
quests.explanation: Opening with something specific to the recipient, rather than your own background, immediately signals the message isn't a mass-sent template.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The business owner replies asking 'what would that actually look like?' Answer with a specific, concrete next step rather than a general pitch.
quests.correctAnswer: I'd start with one post based on a question your customers actually ask you a lot - see how that lands, then go from there if it's a good fit.
quests.hint: Propose a small, specific, low-commitment first step.
quests.explanation: A small, concrete first step is often more persuasive in cold outreach than a full-scale proposal, because it lowers the risk of saying yes.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You're pitching a startup idea to a potential co-founder, not an investor. What should the emphasis shift toward, compared to an investor pitch?
quests.correctAnswer: The shared mission and the specific gap you'd want them to fill, rather than market size and traction numbers.
quests.hint: A co-founder is deciding whether to join you, not whether to invest - the decision criteria are different.
quests.explanation: The same idea needs a genuinely different pitch depending on whether you're asking someone to fund it or to build it with you.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a startup idea - a marketplace for renting specialty tools - to a potential co-founder with strong engineering skills, emphasizing the gap you need them to fill.
quests.correctAnswer: I've got the market and the early customer conversations figured out - what I actually need is someone who can make the booking and payment flow feel effortless, and that's you.
quests.hint: Speak directly to the specific gap this person would fill, not a general pitch of the idea.
quests.explanation: Naming the specific gap a potential co-founder would fill shows you've thought about the partnership, not just the idea in the abstract.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The potential co-founder asks 'what happens to equity if this doesn't work out in six months?' Answer honestly and directly, since trust matters more than enthusiasm here.
quests.correctAnswer: Fair to ask upfront - I'd want a real vesting schedule in writing before we start, so neither of us is stuck if it doesn't work out.
quests.hint: Answer plainly and practically, treating the question as reasonable rather than pessimistic.
quests.explanation: Answering a hard practical question honestly and without defensiveness is often what actually earns a potential co-founder's trust.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You're pitching leadership on the timing of a product launch. What should the pitch balance, beyond just excitement about the product?
quests.correctAnswer: Real risk and readiness alongside the excitement - leadership needs an honest picture, not just enthusiasm.
quests.hint: Leadership is weighing a decision, not just absorbing energy - the pitch needs substance alongside enthusiasm.
quests.explanation: Enthusiasm alone rarely gets a launch approved at the leadership level - the pitch needs to demonstrate the decision has actually been thought through.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a product launch timeline to leadership, balancing genuine excitement with an honest note about remaining risk.
quests.correctAnswer: We're genuinely ready on the core experience, and early testers have responded well - the one open risk is payment processing under high load, which we're stress-testing this week.
quests.hint: Pair the excitement with one honest, specific open risk, rather than presenting a flawless picture.
quests.explanation: Naming one honest, specific risk alongside real excitement tends to build more confidence in leadership than an unqualified 'everything's perfect' pitch.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A leader asks 'what's our fallback if that payment risk doesn't resolve in time?' Answer with a concrete contingency plan.
quests.correctAnswer: If it's not resolved by Thursday, we delay the launch by one week rather than ship something we're not confident in - better a short delay than a bad first impression.
quests.hint: Give a specific, concrete fallback plan rather than vague reassurance.
quests.explanation: Having a real, specific contingency plan ready is what turns an honest risk disclosure into something leadership can actually approve confidently.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You're pitching a volunteer-run community garden project to a group of skeptical residents at a town meeting. What should the pitch avoid leading with?
quests.correctAnswer: An overly polished, corporate-sounding pitch - a community audience often responds better to something that sounds genuinely local and personal.
quests.hint: Match the tone of the pitch to the setting - a town meeting isn't a boardroom.
quests.explanation: A pitch that sounds too polished or corporate can feel out of place, and even suspicious, in a genuinely community-driven setting.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch that community garden project to skeptical residents, in a tone that fits a town meeting rather than a corporate pitch.
quests.correctAnswer: That empty lot on Fifth Street's been sitting there for two years - a few of us think it could actually grow something instead of just collecting trash.
quests.hint: Use plain, direct, local language rather than a polished sales tone.
quests.explanation: Local, plain language, grounded in a specific real place residents recognize, fits this setting far better than a formal pitch structure would.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A resident says 'who's going to maintain it, though? These things always fall apart after the first summer.' Answer honestly, addressing the real, common concern directly.
quests.correctAnswer: That's a fair worry, honestly - we've already got five households committed to a rotating schedule, and it's written down, not just talked about.
quests.hint: Acknowledge the common failure pattern honestly, then show specific evidence you've planned around it.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging a well-known failure pattern honestly, then showing specific evidence you've planned around it, is more convincing than simply promising it'll be different this time.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You're pitching a community mural project to a mixed audience of city officials and local artists in the same room. What tension should the pitch acknowledge?
quests.correctAnswer: Officials likely care about cost, permits, and upkeep, while artists care about creative freedom - the pitch should speak honestly to both without dismissing either.
quests.hint: Two groups in the same room may have genuinely different priorities that need to both be addressed honestly.
quests.explanation: A pitch to a mixed audience with different priorities works best when it names the tension honestly rather than pretending both sides want exactly the same thing.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Deliver the mural pitch, speaking honestly to both the officials' practical concerns and the artists' creative concerns in the same short pitch.
quests.correctAnswer: For the city, this comes with a maintenance plan and a five-year agreement already in writing. For the artists in the room, the design brief is intentionally loose - we want your actual voice, not a committee's version of it.
quests.hint: Give each group a genuine, specific sentence addressing their real priority.
quests.explanation: Addressing two genuinely different priorities honestly, in the same pitch, without watering either one down, is the real test of adapting to a mixed room.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: An artist in the room asks 'so who actually has final approval on the design?' Answer honestly, even if the answer involves a real compromise between the two groups.
quests.correctAnswer: Honestly, it's shared - the city signs off on content and placement, but the actual creative direction stays with the artists. Neither side gets a full veto over the other.
quests.hint: Answer honestly about the real compromise, rather than implying one side has unchecked control.
quests.explanation: A genuine, imperfect compromise between two audiences' interests, named honestly, is more credible than pretending one side simply won.
